title: Sole Defender
description: Inside a narrow crack in the Mother Tree’s massive trunk in Davokar, Agathara makes her third and final attempt to unleash Prios Burning Glass against the Manogal swarm — the only party member to resist all four enthrallment checks while her companions lie paralyzed around her. Kneeling in the cramped passage, golden radiance finally erupts from her hands toward the rearing bat-creatures.
searchHint: "Burning Glass" or "enthrall" or "Mother Tree" or "Manogal"
narrativeSource: Book One, Chapter 19 — The Mother Tree
narrative: She was the only one.

Baldric froze. The warrior’s body locked in mid-motion, his warhammer arrested at the apex of a swing that would never fall, his eyes wide and glassy and seeing nothing. The keening had found the gap in his mental defenses and poured through it, and the man who could shatter armor with a single blow stood motionless as a statue while the things that had frozen him closed the distance.

Reginald went rigid beside her. The scholar’s rapier hung in the air, suspended by a hand that had forgotten how to grip, and his face was blank — the sharp, animated intelligence that normally lit his features extinguished as thoroughly as a candle pinched between thumb and forefinger.

Coriol swayed. The changeling’s eyes went wide, went unfocused, and a sound came from his throat that was not a word but a moan — the sound of a mind being invaded, this time by something that wanted nothing from him except his stillness.
Three of four, paralyzed. Only Agathara standing.
She raised her hands. The Burning Glass formed behind her eyes — the door in the soul, the invitation to the light. She spoke the words. She opened the door.
Nothing happened.

The light that had been building in her palms sputtered, flickered, and died. The words had been right, the intent had been right, but the corruption in the air, the pressure of the keening, the sheer weight of the situation had disrupted the channel, and the Burning Glass had not fired.
The Mangonaals surged forward.
Two pushed past the front line. They came for Agathara.
She tried again. The prayer, the door in the soul. She spoke the words with desperate precision, reaching for the light with everything she had — and fumbled again.

The prayer died in her hands for the second time. Agathara went down — not from the failure, but from the physical manifestation of it. The backlash sent her sprawling, her body striking the bark floor with an impact that drove the breath from her lungs. She lay on her back, staring up at the ceiling of the tree crack, and the Mangonaals loomed above her, their claws raised, their tongues flickering.

Coriol cast the Thorncloak on Agathara. The magic settled over her like a mantle of invisible barbs — a defensive enchantment that did not merely protect but punished, turning the body of the wearer into a weapon that struck back at anything that dared to touch it. The first Mangonaal struck. Its claws raked across her prone body — across the layers of armor, the Blessed Shield, and the Thorncloak. The damage was soaked. Steel and faith and thorns absorbed the blow that should have torn her open.
She would not fail a third time.

She closed her eyes. She reached deeper — past the training, past the seminary, past the careful architecture of Theurgic invocation that she had spent her life learning. She reached for the thing beneath all of that. The reason she had become a Theurg in the first place. The conviction, absolute and unshakable, that the light of Prios was not a tool to be wielded but a truth to be lived, and that truth did not fail. Could not fail. Not here. Not now.
She opened her eyes. She opened the door. She did not speak the words.
The words were unnecessary. The Burning Glass erupted from her body like a star being born.

The radiance filled the corridor. It struck everything corrupt, everything profane, everything that had no right to exist in a world where the sun still rose. The Mangonaals screamed — not the keening, not the hunting cry, but the high, thin sound of things that had encountered something they could not enthrall, could not drain, could not endure.
The enthrallment shattered.

title: The Bridge at Yonderos
description: During the desperate rear-guard defense at Yonderos bridge, Agathara activates Holy Aura and Prios Burning Glass simultaneously — golden aura rings pulse outward across the crumbling stone as waves of blight-born creatures dissolve into light.
searchHint: "Holy Aura" or "bridge" or "blight-born"
narrativeSource: Book Two, Chapter 12 — The World Unravels
narrative: The bridge was six hundred metres long and twenty-five wide — a temporary construction of lashed logs and rope, built across the Dewdram where the old ferry routes had been. Runners with torches lit the braziers along its length, and the firelight revealed the horde.

They came in a mass so dense that the bridge sagged under their weight. The front rank was blight-born humans — corrupted beyond recognition, their acidic blood spraying across anything it touched. Behind them came the clan fiends — flesh-crafted abominations with massive bone spikes erupting from their bodies, carrying two-handed weapons with the mechanical efficiency of things that did not tire.
The defenders formed up. Sappers with grenades, pikemen bracing, archers behind. The party chose the rear guard.
“We’ve got the Agathara of Mass Destruction,” Karano observed, and the dry delivery was so perfectly timed that even Agathara allowed herself the ghost of a smile.

Agathara raised her hands and spoke the words of the Blessed Shield, settling its golden protection over herself, Reginald, and Karava. The troll blinked as the radiance sank into his stone-bark armour — an expression of simple wonder, as though he had not expected grace to feel like warmth.

The horde struck the front line. For fifteen minutes the organised crash of shield and pike held. Then the blight-born overwhelmed the line by sheer numbers, climbing over their own dead. The horns sounded retreat, and the rearguard became the front line.
Then Agathara raised her hands.

The Burning Glass at its fullest power — unleashed without restraint — was not fire. It was judgement made visible. The radiance erupted from her outstretched palms and struck the horde not as a beam but as a wave, rolling across the bridge with the inevitability of dawn. The front row simply ceased to exist — blight-born humans dissolving, vaporising, becoming dust and a cascading ripple of screaming agony that traveled back through the ranks.
Behind the stunned and burning front line, the horde kept coming.

Karava laughed. A low, rumbling chuckle that sounded like gravel and stone knocking together in the belly of the earth. He stepped forward and swung Anthem upward in a rising arc that struck the nearest staggering clan fiend with a force that ignored its armour entirely.

Agathara cast Holy Aura, and the sustained golden emanation rolled outward — burning every abomination in sight, healing every ally. The radiance held — sustained, relentless — searing corruption with each heartbeat and knitting wounded flesh in the same breath.

Then Karava swung. The bridge pitched beneath him at the worst possible moment. Anthem’s blade glanced off his own knee guard, slammed into the bridge planking, and the troll went down on his back in the knee-deep water with a crash that sent spray twenty feet in every direction.
His first battle. His first song. And he had hit himself with his own axe.

But the song did not stop. Lying on his back in the river water, Anthem half-buried in the bridge beside him, Karava kept singing. The vibration continued — through the bridge, through the water, through the stone beneath — because the song was not about the singer. It was about the earth.

title: Audience with the Death Prince
description: Inside the Crown Ship throne room, Agathara stands before the ancient undead Death Prince Cantor Anoreal — seated on the ship’s throne — and offers an otherworldly medallion in her bare hand to purchase the freedom of two Ambrian prisoners from a sunrise sacrifice ritual.
searchHint: "Cantor Anoreal" or "Death Prince" or "medallion"
narrativeSource: Book One, Chapter 17 — The Crown Ship
narrative: Agathara sat with her back against the wall and felt the otherworldly medallion cold against her chest and looked at her companions.
“Can we really let this happen?” she said.

Coriol’s expression was carefully neutral. He would defer to her on this. He always deferred to her on this. Not because he lacked principles, but because his principles were practical and hers were absolute, and when those two frameworks collided, he trusted hers more than his own.
“Whatever you decide,” he said.
“If it doesn’t compromise what we came here to do,” Baldric said slowly, “I won’t stand in the way. But I need you to understand that this is a risk.”

“Some things are simply wrong,” Agathara said. “Watching them happen when you have the power to stop them — that is also wrong. These are our countrymen. They are going to be butchered for the entertainment of dead men who have no right to still be walking, and I will not sit in this room and listen to it happen.”
The words settled into the silence like stones dropped into still water.
“The medallion,” Coriol said after a moment. “We trade the medallion for the prisoners.”

Cantor Anoreal was in his throne room when they found him, seated with the Wraithmark of the Eternity Legion resting on his gauntleted palm. He looked up with the faintly irritated expression of someone interrupted in the act of remembering.

Agathara stepped forward. She held the medallion in both hands, the yellowish-green metal catching the dim light of the ever-burning lamps. It looked alien in her palms — too heavy, too strange, an object that belonged to a sky with three moons and buildings that stretched for hundreds of meters under a deep blue horizon.
“We found this on your ship,” she said. “In the room of the Dacthonic priest. We wondered if it belonged to you — or to the ship, at least. If it once lived here, perhaps it should return.”

Cantor Anoreal looked at the medallion. His gauntleted hand extended, and Agathara placed it on his palm. He turned it over. Examined it. The red light in his eyes shifted, deepened — not nostalgia but recognition.
“Fine,” he said. “They’re your responsibility. Anything they take, anything they do, is now on you and your heads.”

The cages opened with a sound like old bones cracking, and the two Ambrians stumbled out with the bewildered, fragile movements of people who had been preparing to die and were not yet certain they had stopped.

The taller of the two moved immediately to a pile of confiscated belongings and retrieved, with the particular possessiveness of a man reuniting with a piece of his own identity, a rapier. He checked the edge, tested the grip, and slid it into the scabbard at his hip with a motion so practiced it looked involuntary.
“Thank you,” he said. “I am Reginald. My companion is Frank — my manservant, and the only loyal man in that doomed expedition.”
He paused, and something moved behind his eyes — not anger, exactly, but the cold, analytical assessment of a man filing information for future use.
“We would very much like to join your group,” he said. “If you will have us.”
“Welcome,” Agathara said.

title: Flickering Return
description: After fighting abominations alone throughout the city while the party was separated, Aro returns to Nighthome’s entrance hall — his divine light sputtering and phasing, an impaled goblin hanging from a broken window behind him. The cost of sustained solo combat made visible in unstable golden light.
searchHint: "Aro" or "flickering" or "Nighthome"
narrative: They were descending the stairs when the window shattered.

The sound came from the ground floor — the crash of breaking glass, followed by a gurgling screech that cut off abruptly, followed by silence. The party froze on the staircase, weapons drawn, eyes straining in the dim light of the entrance hall below.
A faint golden glow, emanating from somewhere near the front of the building.

Aro Sunspear was in the entrance hall. The spirit templar — Agathara’s patron saint, the golden warrior who had been their distraction and decoy for the crossing of the corrupted city — was crouched near a front window, and through the window, impaled on a jutting shard of glass, was the broken body of a goblin abomination. Aro had driven the creature through the window with enough force to pin it on the glass like an entomologist’s specimen.

Aro himself looked bad. His golden luminescence was flickering, the light stuttering and pulsing in a way that Agathara had never seen. He was damaged — not in the way that living things were damaged, with blood and bruising, but in the way that spiritual manifestations suffered when the forces sustaining them were strained beyond their limits. He had been fighting alone, in a city of abominations, for hours, with nothing but his fists and his faith and the iron resilience of a man who had already died once and was not particularly impressed by the concept.
“Aro,” Agathara said, and the relief in her voice was sharp enough to cut.
The spirit templar looked at her. His expression — insofar as a glowing spirit manifestation could be said to have expressions — was tired.
“I found you,” he said.
“Are you —”
“I will manage. We should leave.”

They descended to the basement, through the storerooms, down the spiral staircase, through the hidden door in the south wall. The center tunnel — earthen, rough-hewn, barely wide enough for Karava’s shoulders — stretched ahead of them into darkness.
They ran.
The air changed. The smell of earth gave way to the smell of growing things — leaf mold and moss and the indefinable green scent that was Davokar, the forest that watched and breathed and remembered.
They emerged into twilight. Beyond the tree line, the forest stretched in every direction — dark, ancient, and alive in a way that the ruined city behind them was not.

Aro flickered beside her, his golden light dimming and brightening in an irregular rhythm that spoke of damage, of strain, of a spirit pushed to the edges of its capacity. She wanted to reach for him — to touch his arm, to offer comfort the way she offered it to the living. But he was not living, and her hand would pass through him, and the gesture would only remind them both of what he had lost.
Aro said nothing, but his light steadied.
They walked into the forest. Behind them, the pillar of darkness still rose from the grave of Thistle Hold, and the cloud spread slowly across the sky like a bruise.
Ahead, Davokar waited. It always waited.

title: Danger Sense
description: Outside a tunnel exit in Davokar, Aro Sunspear begins glowing increasingly brighter — his danger sense triggering as something large approaches the camp from an unexpected direction. Golden form at the edge of the forest, light intensifying against the vast dark of Davokar. The warning before the threat arrives.
searchHint: "Aro" or "glowing" or "danger"
narrativeSource: Book Two, Chapter 16 — The Edge of Davokar
narrative: Karano fell in behind Karava as they moved through the forest, and for a few moments the simple act of walking with companions — of hearing footsteps other than his own, of seeing light that he had not made — was enough to push back the memory of the forest’s patient, shifting attention.
Then Aro began to glow brighter.

Not the steady warmth of the patron saint’s ordinary luminescence — this was something else. The glow intensified in pulses, each pulse throwing longer shadows, each pulse accompanied by a faint trail of mist that streamed behind the spirit like the wake of a ship cutting through still water. Aro stopped walking. His hand went to his sword.
“There is danger ahead,” he said. “Near the camp. Something is approaching from the other direction.”

Karava did not hesitate. He broke into a run — if it could be called running, what a troll did when urgency overcame the careful placement of feet that defined his normal movement. It was more like a controlled avalanche, brush and branches shattering against his shoulders.
Karano ran with him. Aro streaked ahead, his spectral form covering ground in long, floating strides, trailing light like a comet.

They smelled the smoke first. Then they saw the fire — the signal fire, its smoke column visible against the dark sky. The clearing appeared through the trees, and in it, two figures: Agathara with her pike, Reginald with his sword drawn, both facing the direction from which the crashing had come.
Not Karava’s direction. The other direction.

Agathara turned and saw them, and the relief on her face lasted exactly long enough for the sound from the opposite treeline to register — the snapping of branches, the heavy displacement of something large pushing through the undergrowth with the same disregard for silence that Karava showed but with none of his familiarity.
Something else was coming. And Aro’s glow was brighter than Karano had ever seen it.
They stumbled out of the darkness and into the firelight, and they were not monsters.

There were two of them. Tall, gaunt, wearing tattered clothes and bandanas over their faces, their hands empty of weapons though blades hung sheathed at their belts. They moved with the desperate, lurching gait of people who had been running for a long time and had found, at last, something to run toward.
“Help,” one of them said, in a voice thick with something between an accent and a physiology. “We need help.”

Karava had placed himself between the newcomers and the camp with the immovable certainty of a man who had made a promise to cut the next threatening thing in half and intended to keep it. He held Anthem across his body, his dark eyes measuring the strangers with an intensity that suggested he was calculating trajectories.

title: The Opal Storm
description: Crossing the Opal Storm surrounding Othelius Arboretum Island — a corruption-destroying phenomenon that nearly kills the more corrupted party members — Karano walks through it completely unaffected. He carries zero corruption at that moment. The swirling opalescent storm churns around him and cannot touch him.
searchHint: "Opal Storm" or "Karano" or "corruption"
narrativeSource: Book Two, Chapter 11 — The Garden at the End of the World
narrative: The Opal Storm raged at the island’s edge — a wall of screaming light and shattered magic that punished everything tainted, corruption reading the damage in a body and finding its cracks.
Through that wall, without haste or apparent effort, a figure emerged.

He was young, with the unfinished quality of someone whose body had outpaced whatever lived inside it. The storm churned around him — opalescent tendrils of corrupted energy that shredded anything impure — and where it touched him it found nothing to grip. He carried no corruption. He was clean, in the way that only those who had made the Iron Pact and kept it were ever truly clean: not through innocence, but through an act of will so thorough that the forest had agreed to recognize it.

The sword in his right hand burned in the spectral register like a second sun — a resonance that belonged to the bedrock of the world, older than corruption or holiness, forged when the powers that moved through creation were not yet divided into light and dark. He carried it the way a child carries a stick found in a field — loosely, without ceremony, as though its weight were an afterthought.
The storm parted around him. Not blown aside, not overcome — simply parted, the way water parts around a stone that has always been there.

Later, when the island cratered inward and the Opal Storm closed over it like a mouth, the party ran. The crossing was agony — corruption reading their damage, finding their cracks. They survived. They always survived — not through strength or luck but through the stubborn, irrational refusal to die that was the party’s single most consistent trait.

But for Karano, the crossing had been something else entirely. He had walked through the storm untouched. Zero corruption, in a place designed to punish corruption. The Opal Storm found him and found nothing to take.
He never mentioned it. He never spoke of the things the forest did not do to him, only of the things he had done for it.

title: The Impossible City
description: After critically failing a Bushcraft check in Davokar, Karano climbs a tree to orient himself and sees something impossible: Thistle Hold — which supposedly exploded — standing intact on the horizon, its beacon lit and city lights glowing. Hunter in the high forest canopy, through branches: a city that should not exist.
searchHint: "Karano" or "Bushcraft" or "Thistle Hold" or "beacon"
narrativeSource: Book Two, Chapter 16 — The Edge of Davokar
narrative: The forest ate his trail.

He had gone carefully, the way he always went — weight on the balls of his feet, shoulders turned to slip between branches, eyes tracking the ground for spoor and scat and the small signs of life that meant prey nearby. He found no squirrels. He found no rabbits. He found no sign that anything warm-blooded had moved through this stretch of forest in days, and that absence was itself a warning that he registered but could not afford to heed.
He walked deeper. And the forest shifted around him.

He noticed it first as a wrongness in his backtrail. The tree he had passed — the one with the split trunk and the fungal shelf at eye height — should have been behind him and to the left. He turned to check. It was not there. The trail of bent grass and scuffed earth that should have marked his passage had vanished, as though the forest had healed itself behind him the way skin closes over a wound.
He stopped. He breathed. He reached for the calm that a hunter cultivates the way a priest cultivates faith — the still centre from which observation flows.
He was lost.

The knowledge settled in his stomach like cold water. Karano, Ironsworn hunter, tracker and bowman, the man who read terrain the way Reginald read ancient texts — lost in the woods. The forest had taken him, and the taking had been so gentle and so total that he had not felt it happening.

He found a tall tree and climbed. The bark was slick and oddly warm. The branches held his weight but bent in ways he did not expect, as though the wood were not quite solid, not quite convinced of its own rigidity. He climbed past the lower canopy and emerged into the upper reaches where the view opened.

He heard it first: the faint, rhythmic thock of an axe on wood. Distant but real — a sound with source and direction. That was left. That was the direction of camp. He filed the information and turned his head.
And there, to the east, was Thistle Hold.

The beacon burned first in his vision — a column of flame atop the tower, throwing its light against the dusk in the way it had thrown its light for years. Below it, the city spread in the familiar dark outline of walls and rooftops, and as he watched, the evening lights came on. One by one, then in clusters, then in sweeping lines — the warm amber glow of oil lanterns spreading across the streets of a city that was going about the ordinary business of nightfall.
A city that should not have existed. A city they had watched explode.

Karano stared. He tried to marshal the facts: they had seen the corruption blast. They had felt the shockwave in the tunnel. They had emerged to find themselves in a forest that should have bordered a ruin, not a functioning city.

Something was wrong with what he was seeing. He knew this the way he knew the wrongness of the forest — not through logic but through the animal instinct that kept a man alive in places where logic failed.

He climbed down. He filed the information. And he walked toward the sound of chopping, because the sound of chopping was real and the city might not be, and a hunter chose the evidence of his ears over the evidence of his eyes when the eyes had been given reason to lie.

title: Fata Morgana
description: At an illusory oasis in the Alberetor wasteland, mind-controlled by the Fata Morgana lake creature, Karano walks toward the deadly water in a trance — saved at the last moment by Lamerra’s secret undead soldiers emerging from the darkness behind him and grabbing him two steps from the edge.
searchHint: "Fata Morgana" or "mind-control" or "lake" or "undead soldiers"
narrativeSource: Book Two, Chapter 7 — The World That Was
narrative: It appeared without warning — one moment the landscape was the same grey desolation it had been for miles, and the next the trail curved around a low rise and there it was: a pocket of autumn. A small lake, sixty or seventy yards across, glittering in light that seemed to come from nowhere in particular. Trees ringed its banks, their leaves turned to gold and amber and deep rust. The grass was green. The air smelled of earth and water and growing things.
Karano stopped first. His bow was in his hand before the beauty of the scene fully registered, because beauty, in this place, was a warning sign.

They stayed anyway. The water skins were empty. Two days without water in the wasteland of Alberetor was not something even faith could remedy, and the alternative to drinking from this lake was dying of thirst within sight of the one thing in this dead country that still resembled life.

The lake was clean. The berries were clean. Lamerra’s witch sight confirmed it. And so they ate, and drank, and rested in the false autumn that someone had planted here in the grey waste like a hook baited for the starving.

The soldier walked into the lake. He did not hesitate, did not flinch at the cold, did not look back. He waded until the water reached his chest, and then he went under, and the surface closed over his bucket helm without a ripple.
Agathara opened her mouth to shout — and Karano walked past her toward the lake.

He was asleep. His eyes were open but empty, reflecting the false moonlight with a glassy sheen that was not quite consciousness, and his feet moved with the unhurried certainty of a man who knew exactly where he was going. As he walked, his outline began to blur, to soften at the edges — not his own trick, but something else choosing it for him, wrapping him in concealment the way a spider wraps a fly.
“Karano!” Reginald was out of his hammock, rapier drawn. “Karano, stop —”

The two undead soldiers intercepted Karano six feet from the waterline. They tackled him with the graceless efficiency of things that understood force but not restraint, bearing him down into the grass and pinning him there. Karano thrashed. The hunter was strong — Iron Pact strong — and the soldiers struggled to keep him down. His invisibility flickered, failed, returned, failed again.
From the lake came a scream.

Karano went limp. Whatever had been pulling him forward released its grip with the abruptness of a cut wire, and the hunter was suddenly and entirely himself again — pinned to the ground by two walking corpses, staring up at the false sky of a false night in a false valley.
“The lake tried to eat you. My soldiers stopped it.”

Karano looked at the soldiers. Looked at the lake. Looked at his own hands, which were still reaching toward the water, fingers extended, as though some remnant of the compulsion lingered in his muscles.
“They’re sitting on my chest.”
They ran until the oasis was a smudge of false colour behind them. Until the silence was the honest silence of the wasteland rather than the predatory silence of the trap.

“There was no water,” Lamerra said, and his voice was flat. “There was never any water. A sorcerer of extraordinary skill created that entire oasis as a feeding ground. The lake, the trees, the berries. All of it. A trap for anyone desperate enough to drink.”

title: The Impossible Shot
description: On a ridgeline above the Veiled Library, using Master Trick Archery on a critical success — a natural 1 on the die — Karano kills a sorcerer hiding behind rocks with an arrow that bends impossibly around the obstacle. The calligraphic arrow-path curves around cover to reach the sorcerer on the other side.
searchHint: "ricochet" or "trick shot" or "sorcerer" or "cover"
narrativeSource: Book Two, Chapter 9 — The Library That Remembers
narrative: From the ridgeline, sorcery.

The black bolt struck Karano in the chest — a lance of dark energy that ignored his armour entirely and drove him flat against the copper dome. Pain lit every nerve. His muscles locked. He felt the bolt pinning him to the metal surface like a specimen on a board, and the sorcerer on the ridgeline was already preparing a second.

Karano focused. The agony was absolute, the paralysis complete. He focused harder. The world narrowed to a single point of will — not against the magic, but through it — and something inside him turned, and the binding shattered.

He rolled. Drew. His arrow found the sorcerer not through the conventional path — the ridgeline offered excellent cover, natural stone formations that would have stopped a direct shot — but through the improbable path, the one that required the shaft to ricochet off a rock face and change direction mid-flight.
The arrow struck stone, sang, and buried itself in the sorcerer’s throat.

Below, the battle had reached its crisis. Lamerra called on the Subjugator’s deepest power, and a pressure descended on the battlefield, invisible and absolute. Every enemy within the hall simply stopped — weapons frozen mid-swing, feet locked to the floor, eyes wide with the particular terror of men who found their bodies no longer obeyed them.

Agathara cast Lifegiver. The golden radiance erupted from her in a wave, rolling outward, touching every ally. Corruption bled away. Wounds closed. Those on the edge of death drew breath and found, somehow, that they were not yet done.
The shackles broke. The enemies moved. And the battle resumed.

It ended with Agathara stepping into Frederick Ocel’s path. The Burning Glass struck him in the chest — holy light, concentrated to a point, carrying the weight of every prayer she had spoken. The light punched through his armour and found the corruption deep and structural, woven into the fabric of his being like rot through timber.
Frederick Ocel looked down at the light burning in his chest. He looked up at the woman who had put it there.
Then he disintegrated. The dust hung in the air for a long moment, catching the light from the dome above, and then settled like grey snow on the barricade stones.
The remaining enemies broke.

title: Thistle Beast Ambush
description: At a street intersection in the corrupted ruins of Thistle Hold, Reginald engages four massive acidic-blooded thistle beasts largely solo, landing a 14-damage Master Backstab followed by a second 14-damage hit with hypnotic poison. Acid gore soaks his scholar’s robe throughout the fight.
searchHint: "thistle beast" or "Backstab" or "acid"
narrative: Reginald was already among them, and what he did in the next thirty seconds was something Agathara had not seen from him before. Perhaps it was the acid eating through his armor. Perhaps it was simply that Reginald, stripped of his pendant’s invisibility by the corruption that would kill him if he used it, had decided that if he could not hide, he would be the most dangerous thing in the intersection instead.

His rapier opened the first beast’s face from jaw to brow in a single rising cut. The blade reversed, stabbed deep into the shoulder of the second creature as it lunged, and something in the strike — some instinct for the places where flesh was weakest — sent a shudder through the abomination’s body that locked its muscles for a critical, frozen heartbeat. The knife in his off hand was already moving, finding gaps, punishing hesitation.

The second beast lunged with both foreclaws, and Reginald — with the fluid, acrobatic grace that had earned him his reputation — simply stepped aside, redirecting the creature’s momentum so that its claws tore not into him but into its packmate. Corrupted blood sprayed. The disemboweled beast collapsed in a heap of ruptured intestine and acid.
Karano’s arrow took the downed beast through the eye. The hallowed shaft punched clean through bone and brain, delivered with the cool accuracy of a man shooting targets at a festival.
Karava arrived at the fight like weather.

Anthem sang — there was no other word for it, the thundering enchantment on the axe’s head producing a deep, resonant harmonic as it cut the air — and the blade caught the third beast across the ribs with a force that bounced the creature off the cobblestones like a thrown ball. Bones cracked. Limbs snapped at angles that should not have existed.

The fourth beast bit him. A lunging, open-jawed strike that caught him across the shoulder and drove its teeth deep enough to exceed his threshold for pain. Karava staggered. Went to one knee. The beast’s jaws were locked on his shoulder, shaking, the way a dog shakes a rat.
It bled out before it could do more. Reginald’s knife had found its throat from behind, and the creature’s grip slackened as its blood joined the acid-etched ruin of the intersection.

Four thistle beasts. Dead. Agathara stood over the cowering civilians with her thundering pike in a defensive stance, and the noise of the fight was already drawing fresh howls from deeper in the city.
Reginald was soaked. Civilian blood. Beast blood. Acid. He looked down at himself with an expression of weary distaste.
“We need to run,” Agathara said.
They ran.

Emerging from stealth shimmer, rapier extended in killing thrust, bat-creature crumpling.
searchHint: "Omalkin" or "Manigal" or "critical" or "Feint"
narrativeSource: Book One, Chapter 19 — The Mother Tree
narrative: Agathara held. Her faith was her armor, and the keening broke against it the way every assault on her convictions had broken before — not easily, not painlessly, but completely.
“Go,” she said, and her voice was the voice of command. “I will handle the prayers. You handle the killing.”

Reginald moved first. His hand went to the pendant at his throat — Omalkin’s Pendant, the artifact of concealment that had served him in a dozen infiltrations and would serve him now in the most desperate one yet. He pressed the hidden catch, spoke the word of activation, and felt the familiar chill of the enchantment settle over him like a second skin.

He was invisible. Not truly — a careful observer might have caught the distortion in the air where his body displaced space. But the Mangonaals were not careful observers. They were hunting by corruption sense and psychic resonance, and Reginald, wrapped in the pendant’s concealment, was none of those things. He was a ghost with a rapier.
He charged.

Thirty feet of rubble-strewn courtyard. Reginald covered it in a run that was closer to a controlled fall, his feet finding purchase on the shattered flagstones with the sure instinct of a man whose acrobatic training had become indistinguishable from reflex. The Mangonaal did not see him. Did not hear him. Did not feel him until the rapier found the gap between its folded wing and the corded muscle of its neck.

The feint was textbook. A ghost of motion to the left, the dagger flickering, and in the fractional instant of confusion the rapier punched home — through the neck, through whatever served the creature for a spine, and out the other side in a spray of dark ichor. The Mangonaal convulsed once and folded sideways across the rubble, its keening cut off mid-frequency with the abruptness of a snapped string.
One down.
The others turned. The keening intensified — deeper, shifting into registers that could not be blocked. Agathara felt it press against her and pushed back with everything she had.

Baldric stood at the threshold of the tree's crack and raised his warhammer. The weapon had killed a pyromancer once — had caved in the man's skull and drunk something of his art in the process — and the spell still lived in the iron head like an ember that never went out. Baldric felt the familiar heat travel up the haft as he invoked it.
He swept the hammer forward, and Brimstone Cascade poured from the iron head like a river breaking through a dam.

The fire hit four of the five remaining Mangonaals simultaneously — a rolling front of alchemical flame washing across the courtyard with the indiscriminate fury of a natural disaster. Their leathery wings caught fire. Two dropped where they stood, bodies curling inward like paper touched by a match. The other two staggered, burning, claws raking at their own bodies.

title: The Rescue
description: In the same cave near the Ziggurat, while Agathara is pinned prone by a Manigal after a critical defense failure, Reginald counter-attacks and skewers the creature through the heart with his rapier — throwing it backward off her. Rapier arriving from frame-right through the creature’s chest.
searchHint: "prone" or "pinned" or "skewer"
narrativeSource: Book One, Chapter 19 — The Mother Tree
narrative: The enthrallment shattered.

Baldric’s eyes cleared. The glassiness left them, replaced by something that was not confusion but pure, concentrated fury — the rage of a warrior who had been held motionless while his companions were mauled, whose body had been stolen from him by a sound, and who now had it back.
He swung.

The warhammer came around in an arc that started at his hip and ended in the skull of the nearest Mangonaal. The blow was everything the weapon was designed to deliver — devastating, absolute, armor-ignoring. The Mangonaal’s head ceased to exist as a recognizable structure.

Reginald came back to himself with a gasp. The first thing his cleared eyes saw was the Mangonaal that had been draining his blood — still attached, still feeding, its tongue embedded in his neck. He feinted left and drove the rapier home beneath the Mangonaal’s jaw. The parrying dagger followed, punching through the creature’s throat. It dropped without a sound.
And then he saw Agathara.

She was on her back. One of the Mangonaals had pinned her — her polearm gone, her hands up, her armor holding but the creature above her raising a claw for a strike she could not deflect. There was no time to think. There was no thought required.

The rapier arrived from his right hand, through the air, through the gap between the Mangonaal’s wing and ribs, through the creature’s heart. Reginald put his full weight behind it — a running thrust, every inch of his reach committed — and the Mangonaal lurched forward under the impact, was lifted, was thrown back off Agathara in a spray of dark blood, and lay still.
Reginald stood over her, rapier dripping, breathing hard.

Agathara looked up at him from the floor. Her face was grey with exhaustion, bright with something that was not quite gratitude — something deeper, a recognition between people who have survived the unsurvivable together and understand that survival is never free.
Reginald wiped his neck with the back of his hand. His expression was composed. His eyes were not.

title: The Coded Library
description: In the third-floor library of Mayor Nightpitch’s manor in Nighthome — every book spine-coded in a 5-letter cipher — Reginald searches exhaustively and arrives at an unwelcome conclusion: the cipher key was never written down. Nightpitch memorized it.
searchHint: "cipher" or "library" or "Nightpitch"
narrative: The library was behind the third door, and Reginald’s eyes brightened at the sight of it despite everything. A research library with a card catalog, a writing desk, shelves of volumes arranged with the careful organization of a man who valued knowledge the way others valued gold.

The index cards were everywhere. Scattered across the floor, the desk, the shelves — hundreds of small rectangles of stiff paper, each one bearing a sequence of five letters at the top and, beneath that, rows of numbers and symbols. Triangles. Diamonds. Colored-in squares. A system that was clearly organized, clearly comprehensive, and clearly incomprehensible to anyone who did not possess its cipher.

Reginald gathered a handful and studied them with the focused intensity that characterized his best scholarly work. His memory was absolute — once he read a thing, he possessed it forever, every stroke of every glyph committed to a mental archive that never faded and never erred. But memory was useless without context, and the cards offered none.

He searched for the key. Methodically, thoroughly, with the patience of a man who had once spent three weeks reconstructing a burned manuscript from its ash patterns. He searched the desk drawers, the false bottom he found in the second drawer, the hollow book on the third shelf, the locked cabinet whose lock he picked in under a minute. He searched with the specific, practiced desperation of someone who knows the answer must be here — it always is, the key is always somewhere — and who cannot afford to be wrong.
“He coded everything,” Reginald said at last. “The entire library. Every book, every reference, every piece of knowledge in this room is filed under a personal cipher that exists nowhere on paper.”
“You are certain?” Agathara asked.

Reginald looked at her with the flat certainty of a man who had just conducted the most thorough search of his career. “I have looked. Thoroughly. The cipher key is not in this room. It is not written down anywhere. Mayor Nightpitch memorized his entire cataloging system.” He paused, allowing the implication to settle. “If we want to know what is in this library — what might help us understand what is happening to this world — we need to find him. In person. Alive.”
The building shuddered. Glass fell and shattered from the room next door. The tremors were coming faster now, each one stronger than the last.

Reginald looked at the shelves one last time. At the hundreds of volumes whose spines bore five-letter codes that meant nothing without the key locked inside a man’s head. At the knowledge that was here and was not here — present in every fiber of every page, inaccessible as a dream.
He turned away. He did not look back.

title: Witch Sight Awakens
description: In the Veiled Library, Reginald’s Witch Sight opens for the first time — a wall crumbling within him — and he sits down and weeps as the library springs to life around him in layered glowing knowledge-light. Amber, silver, and violet light bloom from the stacks as the world reshapes itself around his new perception.
searchHint: "Witch Sight" or "Veiled Library" or "weeping"
narrativeSource: Book Two, Chapter 9 — The Library That Remembers
narrative: The Veiled Library opened beneath them like a flower.

Rooms. Halls. Corridors. Shelves stretching floor to ceiling, loaded with books and scrolls and artifacts arranged with a librarian’s obsessive geometry. Weapons mounted on walls. Jewellery in glass cases. And all of it invisible — hidden behind a mystical veil that turned the air to opacity, so that without witch sight the rooms were simply darkness, and the shelves were simply walls, and the treasures of an empire were simply absence.
Lamerra let go of Agathara’s wrist and stepped fully into the room. The others lost him.

For Agathara, the world became darkness and silence and the terrible sensation of standing in a space she could not perceive. No walls. No floor she could trust. No light, no shadow, no reference point. She reached for the stair railing and found nothing. Her breath came fast.
Then Lamerra was back, and the world returned in a rush of sensation.

“The library is here,” Lamerra said. There was wonder in his voice, and the wonder was more unsettling than any danger would have been, because Lamerra did not wonder at things. “All of it. Perfectly preserved. We just need eyes to see it.”
He looked at each of them in turn. His gaze settled on Reginald.
Reginald moved through the library with the careful, reverent pace of a man in a museum. He stopped before a label that read DEATH OF UNATOR CORONAR.
“The king’s death,” he said. His voice was very quiet. “There is no record of how Coronar died. It’s one of the great mysteries of the last century.”
“Don’t,” Agathara said.
He touched the skull.

The memory took him completely. A throne room — grander, older. A man on the throne: old, tired, wearing a crown that sat on his brow like a migraine. Before him, a figure in a dark cloak, moving with the unhurried pace of someone who had already won. The figure spoke a word. The king’s body seized. Shadows poured from his mouth and nose and eyes, and the king did not scream. He stared at the cloaked figure with an expression of such weary recognition that it was clear he had expected this.

The memory ended. Reginald staggered. Corruption flooded through him — the price of touching a preserved moment — and Agathara was there, her hands on his shoulders, the warm light of her power washing the worst of it away.
“Someone killed him,” Reginald said. His face was grey. “I saw it. A figure in a cloak. He didn’t even fight back.”

Then Lamerra found the sword. His hand closed on the grip. The trap detonated — not fire, not light, but corruption, pure and weaponised, erupting from the blade in a wave that struck everything in the room. Reginald screamed. The blight marks on his hands blazed dark. His face distorted — jaw extending, veins blackening, something pushing outward from beneath his skin that was not him and was not human and was very, very close to breaking through.
Agathara’s light reached him, poured into him, pulled him back from the threshold.
His face reformed. The veins faded. The jaw receded. He was himself again — shaking, sweating, his hands blistered with shadow — but himself.

title: The Chrysalis
description: Agathara erupts from a hollowed Kotkas bear-construct in Brighthaven's fortress atrium, tearing free of the dead flesh and unleashing divine light against the undead guards in a moment of violent liberation.
narrative: Then Lamerra hollowed out the Kotkas.

He did it with his hands and his knife and a kind of grim, surgical focus that none of them wanted to watch but none of them could look away from. The bear-constructs stood motionless while he worked, obedient even as he gutted them, and the cavity he carved in each was just large enough for a person to curl inside. It was warm in there. It was wet. The smell was beyond description.
"No," Agathara said.
"It is the only way past the gates. The undead will not question two Kotkas accompanying an emissary. They will question a living Theurg of Prios walking through their front door."
"Lamerra, I refuse to --"
"Agathara." His voice was gentle, which was worse. "I have been inside worse things. This is a body. A dead one. It will not hurt you. It will carry you."
She looked at the hollowed-out Kotkas. She looked at Lamerra. She looked at the fortress on the ridge, and the army between them and it, and the tower where the map waited.
She climbed inside.

The Kotkas closed around her. The darkness was total. The stench was absolute. She pressed her face into the crook of her arm and breathed through her sleeve and felt the creature begin to move, each step a rolling, lurching gait that pressed its dead flesh against her from every side, and she thought: I have survived blight storms and blood elves and the revelation that my scripture is a lie. I can survive this.

Karano, in the other Kotkas, said nothing. He endured it the way he endured everything -- with silence and the particular patience of a hunter who understood that discomfort was a temporary state and death was not.

The atrium was tall and dim, lit by torches that burned without smoke -- corruption-fed flames that cast shadows in directions no natural fire would produce. Five guards stood at the base of a spiral staircase. They turned at the sound of the door.
"Inspection," Lamerra said. "Apostle Keen's orders."

It was a terrible lie. The guards were not fooled. But Lamerra was already drawing his sword, and the black flames were already licking along its edge, and the first guard fell before the others understood that diplomacy had ended.

Agathara burst from the Kotkas like a chrysalis shattering. The dead flesh parted around her -- she tore it, clawing through the cavity walls with a strength born of equal parts desperation and fury -- and she emerged covered in gore, her battle robes slicked with undead ichor, and her hands were already raised, and the light of Prios erupted from her palms in a wave that filled the atrium.
"THE ANCIENT ENEMY IS HERE!" one of the guards screamed, and the cry echoed upward through the tower, floor after floor. "THE QUEEN AND HER GUARDS HAVE RETURNED!"
They thought she was Korinthia. Of course they did. A living woman emerging inside their fortress, wreathed in holy light -- who else could it be?

The aura hit the undead guards like a physical force, searing through armour, through binding, through bone. Two dropped immediately. The others staggered, the binding that held their bones together fraying under the assault of divine light.

Karano emerged from his Kotkas with considerably more composure than Agathara, rolling free of the dead flesh and coming up with an arrow nocked before his feet touched the ground. The shaft took a guard in the eye socket and punched through the back of the skull, and the undead soldier disassembled with the clatter of a puppet whose strings had been cut.

title: The Gargoyle’s Prayer
description: Agathara comes back to herself crouched over Baldric's dying body, blood on her hands and fangs still visible, and stretches out trembling hands to pray over the man she has harmed -- the vampathera arc.
narrativeSource: Book One, Chapter 13 — Dawn of the Black Sun
narrative: She was crouching over a body. There was blood in her mouth -- warm, salt-copper, still fresh -- and the body beneath her was Baldric's, and he was not moving, and his face was the color of old wax, and his blood was everywhere, on her hands, on her chin, pooling on the flagstones in a spreading dark mirror that reflected the hellish red light of the spell building above the cathedral.

Her companion. Her friend. The man who had carried her through this nightmare, who had borne her weight and her violence and her hunger without complaint, who had positioned himself between her and a demon from the Yonder World because that was what he did, because that was who he was. He lay on the ground at her feet, and he was dying, and she had done this.

The nightmare bane -- the deep-rooted, marrow-level fear that she carried like a splinter in her soul, the terror of watching a companion fall and being unable to stop it -- cracked through the blood-fog in her mind like sunlight through stained glass. For one impossible, crystalline moment, the hunger retreated entirely, and Agathara Silvershade was wholly, completely herself.
She stretched out her hands.

They were shaking. They were covered in Baldric's blood. And she did not know, in that moment, whether Prios would answer. She had been made into something with fangs. She had drunk the blood of the man she was trying to heal. She had been a monster. What god would answer the prayer of a monster?
Prios answered.

The light came as it always came -- warm, golden, an absolute counter to the corruption-saturated darkness of the compound. It flowed through her shaking, blood-covered hands and into the body of the man beneath her, and she felt his wounds close, felt the color return to his flesh, felt his heart strengthen from a faltering stutter to a steady rhythm. Every drop of grace she had left, poured out in a single desperate act of faith and contrition.

Baldric's eyes opened. He looked up at her -- at the blood on her face, at the fangs still visible behind her lips, at the luminous eyes that were, for this one moment, also Agathara's eyes -- and he reached for her hand.
"Can you run?" he asked.
"I don't know for how long."
"Then we run until you can't."

title: The Living Sun
description: At Castle Thorn, Agathara opens herself fully to Prios and the Burning Glass erupts from her hands as a column of absolute sunlight, striking down twelve corrupt soldiers in a single breath.
narrativeSource: Book Two, Chapter 1 — The Throne Without Thorns
narrative: Agathara knelt again. She closed her eyes against the firelight, against the chaos, against the sick wrongness of corruption that had been seeping into her bones since they entered this dead fortress. She did not try a small prayer this time. She did not ask for a shield or a ward or a gentle light.
She opened herself to the sun.

Not commanding -- asking. The way she had been taught, in the seminary in Yndaros, before she had learned that faith was not a weapon but a door. She placed her hands flat on the corrupted stone of Castle Thorn and she asked, and the silence inside her was the silence of a woman who had walked into the heart of darkness and still believed that light existed.
It answered.

The Burning Glass manifested as a column of radiance that had nothing to do with fire. It was sunlight -- concentrated, absolute, the kind of light that left no shadow and brooked no argument. It erupted from Agathara's outstretched hands and filled the dome, and everything it touched that carried corruption in its blood burned.
It was not flame. It was judgment.

A Ranger facing Reginald threw his hands over his eyes as his skin cracked and peeled, the corruption hidden in his blood igniting from within. On the dais, three of the mages toppled sideways, their defensive wards shattering like glass against light that was older than wards and stronger than glass. The rebel soldiers -- those who had drunk from dark wells, who had bargained for power in the places where corruption pooled like standing water -- simply fell.
Twelve of them. Perhaps more. Gone in a breath.

title: Two Faiths at the Fire
description: Agathara and the undead knight Nightblade stand facing each other with the anti-corruption aura burning between them -- two women who served the same god and were each abandoned by the same church.
narrative: Nightblade dismounted. She was taller than Lamerra, taller than Karano -- an imposing figure in scarred plate armour, moving with the deliberate economy of the undead who retained their martial skill. Her visor was raised. Beneath it, her face was what undeath had made of it: preserved but wrong, the skin too tight, the eyes too deep, the expression fixed in a calm that was not peace but its opposite.
She looked at Agathara.
Agathara looked at her.

The light of the anti-corruption aura burned between them -- Agathara's faith, a living sun, and Nightblade's existence, a thing made of the very corruption that sun existed to destroy. The aura pressed against Nightblade like a physical force. She endured it. She did not step back.

"You are the Theurg," Nightblade said. Her voice was dry, uninflected, the voice of a woman speaking through a throat that no longer needed air. "Lamerra writes of you. He says you are the finest servant of Prios he has known."
"And you," Agathara said. Her voice shook. "You are the knight."
"I was a knight." Nightblade's hand rested on the pommel of her greatsword. "What I am now has no name the church would recognize."
"He told us. What happened to you. What the church did." Agathara stopped. Started again. "Was it true? That they abandoned you? That you wrote for help, and no one came?"
"I wrote seventeen letters," Nightblade said. "Three were answered. The answers said to pray harder."

Something in Agathara's face broke and reformed into a different shape. Not forgiveness -- she was not ready for that, might never be -- but recognition. The recognition of a woman who served the same god and who understood, in her bones, what it meant to cry out to heaven and hear nothing but the echo of your own voice.
"Peace was stolen from me," Nightblade said. "The Dark Lords left nothing to rest for. If this form lets me strike them down, I will bear its curse."

title: Beacon in the Dead City
description: Aro materializes at the base of Thistle Hold's beacon tower in the dead city, strobing gold like a lantern in a hurricane and drawing every creature in Toad Square toward him.
narrative: They circled the city to the north gate, near the beacon. Aro was sent ahead -- the closest thing to a perfect scout that Agathara's faith had ever produced. He was to reach the beacon, determine if survivors remained, and report back.
He did not execute this plan with distinction.

The patron saint materialized at the base of the tower, blinking in and out of visibility to catch the attention of anyone watching from above. Rather than a subtle signal, Aro strobed like a lantern in a hurricane -- flashing gold, then gone, then gold again, a beacon beneath the beacon that every creature in Toad Square could see.

A roar split the silence. From around the corner of the tower, a massive figure in the tattered remnants of sun-yellow theurge's robes came charging -- a blight beast, but unlike the mindless horrors that prowled the streets. This one moved with purpose. Its eyes held intelligence.
"Fresh food," it said, in a voice that still remembered human speech. "Substance."

Aro climbed. The rope ladder caught and swung wildly as the creature slammed into its base, but the patron saint's spirit-born strength held, and he hauled himself up hand over hand with the desperate speed of a man outrunning death. Below, the blight beast seized the ladder and began to climb.
The survivors cut the rope.

title: Tearing the Wraith Apart
description: As Karava's troll battle-chant breaks the wraith's terror and Karano puts a hallowed arrow through her face, Aro catches her with a backhand strike that rips her torso apart in a spray of spectral light.
narrative: Karava stood in the wraith's presence with his eyes clear and his heart pounding and his axe in his hands, and the room trembled with the sound of his voice.
He swung. The axe should have split the wraith from crown to sternum. Instead the stroke went wide at the worst possible moment, and Karava buried it in his own foot.
Green ichor erupted across the floorboards. The troll staggered, looked down at the severed extremity, and roared -- not in fear, but in sheer disbelieving outrage.

Karano, shaking free of his terror at the sound of the troll chant, put a hallowed arrow through the wraith's face. The enchanted shaft punched through her vaporous skull and tore a hole in the flickering substance of her form. She screamed in anger, her head reforming around the wound, but the damage was real -- she was thinning, losing coherence. Aro, golden and furious, caught her with a backhand strike that ripped her torso apart in a spray of spectral light.
Through all of this, Karava's foot was regrowing.

The regeneration was grotesque and wonderful in equal measure. The severed foot, retrieved and pressed against the stump of the ankle, began to knit. There was a grinding, squelching crunch as bone found bone and flesh reached for flesh, and then the troll was flexing his toes experimentally, grunting in satisfaction. He picked up his axe.
"There we go," he said. "Good as new."

title: Thorn Cloak Rising
description: As Agathara's Holy Aura floods the camp with light that heals friend and foe alike, Coriol activates his thorn cloak to full strength -- a shimmer of green-tinged energy that turns his body into a weapon against any creature that dares to touch him.
narrative: Holy Aura was light and life together -- a radiance that spilled from Agathara's outstretched hands and filled the clearing with a warm, golden glow that drove the shadows back to the treeline. The camp became visible: bedrolls strewn, weapons drawn, mare cats frozen in the sudden illumination with their pupils constricted to slits and their bodies taut with the instinct to flee from the thing they most feared.

But the Aura was a double gift, and its second edge cut both ways. The healing radiance mended torn flesh and soothed damaged muscle -- in friend and foe alike. The mare cats that had taken wounds felt their injuries close, their confidence return.

"That's healing them too," Coriol observed, his sword and parrying dagger already in hand, his thorn cloak manifesting around him as a shimmer of green-tinged energy that made the air around his body ripple. He had activated the enchantment at its full strength; any creature that struck him would find its own flesh torn by phantom thorns.
"I know," Agathara said. "But now you can see."

The mare cats were learning. They were pack hunters -- intelligent, adaptive, accustomed to bringing down prey through coordinated assault. But the prey before them would not go down. The armored ones shrugged off their attacks. The glowing one healed herself even as she healed them. The one wrapped in phantom thorns punished every touch. And the short one with the enormous sword fought like something that had been killing things since before the cats' grandmothers were kittens.

One by one, the cats peeled away. First the wounded, slinking into the undergrowth to nurse their injuries. Then the cautious, those whose instincts told them that the cost of this hunt exceeded its reward.

title: We May Be Surrounded
description: On the road to Ravenia, Coriol notices that eight of the snow drifts around a dead courier are wrong -- they sit in places where no natural drift would form -- and quietly signals the party before the first one stands up.
narrativeSource: Book One, Chapter 1 — The Road to Ravenia
narrative: It was midafternoon when they heard the scream.

A man's voice -- ragged, desperate, the kind of sound that came from the throat of someone in genuine extremity. It cut through the still winter air from somewhere ahead, perhaps two hundred yards, where the road curved through a grove of bare-branched oaks.

Baldric was moving before the echo died. Gibraltar surged forward at a touch of his knees, the warhorse responding to urgency the way a blade responds to the hand that draws it. The rest of the party tightened formation instinctively -- Flare moving up from the rear, Coriol and Igni closing in on the priests, Agathara reaching for the sun medallion at her throat.

A horse lay sprawled across the road, its legs at wrong angles, a deep gash across its neck and shoulder crusted with dark blood. Beside it, crumpled face-down in the churned snow, a man. A courier, from the look of his riding clothes. Baldric reined Gibraltar to a halt and scanned the treeline. Nothing moved. Nothing made a sound. The silence was total -- not the comfortable silence of a winter forest, but the held-breath silence of a place where something was watching.
Coriol said nothing. He was looking at the snow.

The road here passed through a stretch of woodland, oaks and birches bare of leaves, the ground covered in a smooth white blanket broken only by the usual drifts and hollows. But some of the drifts were wrong. They sat in places where no natural drift would form -- on flat ground, in the lee of nothing, spaced at irregular intervals on both sides of the road in a rough ring around the dead courier and his horse.
He counted them. Eight.
"We may be surrounded," Coriol said, very quietly. "The snow. Those lumps that should not be there."

He made a hand signal -- danger, circle, many -- and saw understanding flash across Baldric's face. The warrior rose from his crouch, slowly, his sword loose in his grip, his eyes tracking the perimeter.
Behind them, Liturge Boreal gasped.
One of the snow lumps was standing up.

title: What the Corruption Knows
description: When two wraiths exhale dark breath toward Coriol, the corruption already saturating his blood resonates with theirs -- the darkness finds kinship, and instead of harm, Coriol feels his wounds ease.
narrativeSource: Book One, Chapter 1 — The Road to Ravenia
narrative: Two of the entangled wraiths raised their hands toward Coriol and exhaled -- not air, but a reeking blast of something cold and dark and ancient, a wind that carried corruption like a plague carries fever. It struck him full in the chest. He braced for agony.
Instead, he felt warmth.

The corruption in his blood -- the accumulated weight of weeks of witch-magic and desperate spellcasting, so much taint that it had become as familiar as his own heartbeat -- resonated with the wraiths' darkness. Instead of adding to his burden, the black breath found kinship with what was already there, and the collision produced not damage but a strange, discordant healing. He felt his bruises ease. Felt the ache in his joints recede.
The wraiths seemed confused. They tried again. Again, Coriol was healed.

Igni was not so fortunate. The same black breath struck the pyromancer like a wall of ice, and because his corruption was low -- barely a trace, the residue of a single misfired spell -- the darkness had nothing to bond with. It piled corruption onto him instead, a flood of taint that rushed through his veins like ice water, and he staggered, gasping, as the shadows bloomed beneath his skin like ink dropped in water.
"Crossbow," he said, through teeth that would not stop chattering. "I'm using the crossbow from now on."

title: Pain Is Negotiable
description: In Nighthome, Karano wakes with broken ribs, takes his bow without a word, and goes forward into the dark -- leading the party through a dead city with the stubbornness of a man who knows pain is negotiable and death is not.
narrative: The party was pressed into the mouth of an alley in the back streets -- Agathara at the rear with the surviving civilians huddled between her and the others, Karano somewhere ahead in the murky half-light with his bow drawn, Reginald a shadow among shadows, and Karava's enormous shape filling the alley's far end like a cork in a bottle. They had been moving for hours through a city that had become an abattoir. Blood on every surface. Buildings smashed, windows shattered, doors ripped from their hinges with a violence that spoke of strength beyond reason.

The corruption pressed against Agathara's skin like ice water that would not drain. In any normal circumstance, the taint would have dissipated within minutes, bleeding off like heat from cooling metal. Here, in this saturated ruin, it clung. It accumulated. And every spell she cast would add not just its normal cost but an additional surge of corruption that could push any of them across the threshold from which there was no return.
Magic was a weapon she could not afford to draw.

"Clear," Karano murmured from the next intersection, his voice barely a breath. He had woken an hour into their flight through the alleys, draped over Karava's shoulder like a sack of grain, his ribs grinding and his vision doubled. Agathara had set the shoulder and bound the ribs with strips torn from a dead man's shirt -- field medicus, no magic, because the corruption cost of healing in this place was a price none of them could pay. The hunter had said nothing. He had taken his bow from Karava's hand, nocked an arrow, and gone forward into the dark with the particular stubbornness of a man who understood that pain was negotiable and death was not. He had been extraordinary since -- rolling forward through the maze of back streets with the focused precision of a man who understood that a single misstep meant death for five civilians who had no other protector. His vigilance had kept them alive. His restraint had kept them silent.

title: The Wraith’s Face
description: Karano breaks free of the wraith's terror at the sound of Karava's battle chant and puts a hallowed arrow through the wraith's face, tearing a hole in her flickering form.
narrative: Karava stood in the wraith's presence with his eyes clear and his heart pounding and his axe in his hands, and the room trembled with the sound of his voice.
He swung. The axe should have split the wraith from crown to sternum. Instead the stroke went wide at the worst possible moment, and Karava buried it in his own foot.
Green ichor erupted across the floorboards. The troll staggered, looked down at the severed extremity, and roared -- not in fear, but in sheer disbelieving outrage.

Karano, shaking free of his terror at the sound of the troll chant, put a hallowed arrow through the wraith's face. The enchanted shaft punched through her vaporous skull and tore a hole in the flickering substance of her form. She screamed in anger, her head reforming around the wound, but the damage was real -- she was thinning, losing coherence.
It was only afterward, huddled in a cold thicket with no fire and no roof, that Karano made the observation that would haunt them.
"The wraith didn't actually hurt anyone," he said. "The only damage was self-inflicted."

title: Three Arrows, One Draw
description: When a blood elf uses an oak pew as a shield to advance on the party, Karano draws and fires three arrows simultaneously -- striking hand, chest, and throat in a single volley of hallowed golden light.
narrative: Three blood elves burst from behind the altar, sprinting down the central aisle. But as they passed the first row of pews, the lead elf seized an entire oak pew -- two hundred pounds of carved mountain timber -- and ripped it from its floor bolts with one hand. It held the pew vertically like a shield, and the other two fell in behind it, and they charged.
The pew blocked the light.

Agathara's Holy Aura filled the chapel with golden radiance that burned everything corrupt within its reach. But the blood elves had watched the party fight the Dragon. They knew what Agathara could do. Behind the pew, they spider-crawled low to the ground, staying below the rays of light that streamed over the pew's upper edge, moving with a fluidity that belonged to the dark between the trees.
"That's devious," Karano said, and drew.

Three arrows. One draw. Karano's volley struck the pew-holding elf in hand, chest, and throat simultaneously. Three bursts of hallowed golden light tore through the corrupted body. The blood elf fell. The pew-shield clattered to the flagstones.

title: Becoming the Abyss
description: A blood elf's fifth corrupting touch drives Reginald past his threshold -- his jaw distends, black veins rise through his skin like roots through soil, and the corruption crosses the boundary from accumulation to transformation.
narrative: Each time a blood elf's hand touched his skin -- not the blade, the hand, pale elongated fingers reaching past his guard to press against the gaps in his armour -- he felt it. Not pain. Worse than pain. A coldness that entered through the skin and sank into the marrow, a wrongness that settled in his blood like silt settling in still water. The blood elves' touch carried corruption the way a plague carrier carries disease, and each contact pushed a little more of that freezing darkness into his body.
The first touch added a whisper. The second added a word. The third added a sentence.

By the fourth touch, Reginald could feel the corruption pooling inside him like black water filling a well. He carried five permanent marks already, from the pendant's use and the accumulated exposure of months in corrupted lands. His threshold was ten -- not generous, but it had not needed to be. Until now.
A fifth touch. He felt it breach.
The corruption crossed the threshold and the world changed.

It was not gradual. It was a switch -- a boundary between what he had been and what he was becoming, and the crossing of that boundary was accompanied by a sound that existed only inside his head: a roaring, rushing noise, like a river breaking through a dam, like something vast and dark and hungry finally given permission to feed.

His bones ached. Not the ache of injury but the ache of change -- of things shifting inside him, rearranging, making room for something that had not been there before. His jaw clenched and then opened too wide, the muscles of his face pulling in directions they had never pulled, and he felt his canine teeth push outward -- not growing but protruding, the gums receding, the enamel lengthening as though his skull were reshaping itself around a mouth that needed to hold more teeth, that needed to open wider.

Black veins appeared on his hands. They rose to the surface of his skin like roots pushing through soil, dark and tarry and pulsing with a rhythm that was not his heartbeat but something else, something that had its own cadence, its own intentions. The veins spread up his forearms, branching and multiplying, a network of dark rivulets tracking through his flesh like ink through water.

His face was the worst. He could feel it changing -- the skin pulling back from his mouth, the jaw distending, the cheekbones sharpening into ridges that pressed outward against skin that was no longer thick enough to contain them.
Reginald screamed.

title: Four Beasts
description: Reginald engages four thistle beasts in Nighthome with nothing but his rapier and knife, redirecting one creature's momentum into its packmate and fighting with lethal precision.
narrative: Reginald crashed into its flank before it completed the turn. His rapier found the junction of head and neck on the nearest skull, and the blade went in with the particular sound of steel entering dense, corrupted flesh.
The creature's blood sprayed in an arc. It hissed where it struck stone. It hissed where it struck Reginald.
"Acid," Karano said from behind her, very quietly.

The beast roared -- a bass note that resonated in the chest -- and three more of its kind came pounding out of the alley behind it. Bear-sized abominations with hides like boiled leather, each one bristling with bone spurs and horn, each one trailing a reek of corrupted bile that made her eyes water.

Reginald was already among them. His rapier opened the first beast's face from jaw to brow in a single rising cut. The blade reversed, stabbed deep into the shoulder of the second creature as it lunged, and something in the strike sent a shudder through the abomination's body that locked its muscles for a critical, frozen heartbeat. The knife in his off hand was already moving, finding gaps, punishing hesitation.

The second beast lunged with both foreclaws, and Reginald -- with the fluid, acrobatic grace that had earned him his reputation -- simply stepped aside, redirecting the creature's momentum so that its claws tore not into him but into its packmate. Corrupted blood sprayed. The disemboweled beast collapsed in a heap of acid.
Karano's arrow took the downed beast through the eye. The hallowed shaft punched clean through bone and brain, delivered with the cool accuracy of a man shooting targets at a festival.

Karava arrived at the fight like weather. Anthem sang -- there was no other word for it, the thundering enchantment on the axe's head producing a deep, resonant harmonic as it cut the air -- and the blade caught the third beast across the ribs with a force that bounced the creature off the cobblestones like a thrown ball. Bones cracked. Limbs snapped at angles that should not have existed.

title: Glass and Morning Light
description: Reginald opens an ancient chest to find four glass cylinders engraved with pre-Symbarian cuneiform -- and holds one to the morning light, already entering the trance of a scholar who has found something that changes everything.
narrativeSource: Book Two, Chapter 13 — The Book of Lies
narrative: The chest resisted. Then something clicked -- a sound like a mechanism releasing, ancient and precise -- and the lid flew open. Inside, resting in moulded crimson velvet, were four glass cylinders.

They were beautiful. Slender rods of clear glass, each the length of a man's forearm, engraved with cuneiform script so intricate and so precise that it seemed to have been etched by something finer than any human tool. The engravings caught the morning light and scattered it in patterns that danced across the velvet lining.
Reginald's breath left him in a sound that was not quite a word.
"They are glass rods," Deceeba observed.
"They are everything," Reginald whispered, and reached for one.

The glass was cool beneath his fingers. Smooth, impossibly smooth, with a faint tingling sensation -- the ghost of something that was not quite warmth and not quite vibration, as though the rod itself were alive at a frequency too low for human perception. He lifted it from the velvet cradle and held it to the light, turning it slowly, watching the cuneiform inscriptions scroll past like text on a prayer wheel.

"The script flows in one direction down each rod," he said, his voice taking on the particular flatness of a scholar entering a state of total concentration. "The opening symbols on each are similar -- a shared prefix, perhaps a classification system." He rotated a rod, comparing it against its neighbour. "The style is reminiscent of early Symbalist ritual notation. Pre-Symbarian. From the era when Symbolism was used only for protection and preservation."

title: The Invisible Strike
description: While Lamerra and Agathara create chaos at the front of Brighthaven's fortress, Reginald slips through invisible, opens three locks in silence, and reappears with his rapier wet and a guard already crumpled at his feet.
narrative: The scholar had gone ahead, invisible, the Omalkin pendant's magic rendering him a ghost among ghosts. He had slipped through the gate behind the party, pressed against the wall, moving with the particular silence of a man who had been practising his entire life for exactly this kind of madness. His invisible hands found the first lock. Tumblers turned. The second lock. The third.
The door opened.
Lamerra sent the Dragouls forward as a distraction, then: "Now."
They entered the tower. Five guards stood at the base of a spiral staircase. They turned at the sound of the door.

It was a terrible lie. The guards were not fooled. But Lamerra was already drawing his sword, and the black flames were already licking along its edge, and the first guard fell before the others understood that diplomacy had ended.
Agathara burst from the Kotkas like a chrysalis shattering, her hands already raised, the light of Prios erupting from her palms in a wave that filled the atrium.
Karano emerged from his Kotkas with considerably more composure, rolling free of the dead flesh and coming up with an arrow nocked before his feet touched the ground.

Reginald appeared from nowhere. The pendant's magic fell away and he was simply there, rapier wet, standing over a guard who had crumpled at the base of the stairs without anyone hearing him fall. He looked at the carnage, at the holy light, at Agathara's gore-streaked face and Karano's notched arrow and Lamerra's burning sword, and he said, "I got the one on the left."

title: Skin Like Diamonds
description: After Agathara invokes the Blessed Defense over the party, its opalescent glass dust sifts down and clings to them like frost, leaving every one of them faintly sparkling — a catastrophe for a group about to sneak across the ruined park beneath the drifting Five Sisters. Worse still, she chose today of all days to wear the unbuttoned sleeveless shirt, and spends the entire crossing clutching it shut with one hand while her glittering skin betrays her at every step.
searchHint: "Blessed Defense" or "sparkle" or "Five Sisters" or "crossing" or "cylinder"
narrativeSource: Book Two — The Node and the Hold
narrative: The third cylinder Agathara did not break on stone.
